intro: Tyler Arboretum, outside Media in Delaware County, still keeps 21 plants that the Painter brothers set out between the 1840s and the 1860s. Three of them are here. A giant sequoia counted the largest in Pennsylvania lost its top in 1895 and grew several spires in its place. A ginkgo stands behind Lachford Hall. And the state's champion Cedar of Lebanon is in decline, by the arboretum's own account. Tyler charges admission, and from Center City Philadelphia it is well over half an hour by public transport, nearer an hour or more.
meta_description: Three Painter-era trees at Tyler Arboretum near Media, PA: Pennsylvania's largest giant sequoia, a ginkgo and a champion Cedar of Lebanon.
question_meta: Tyler Arboretum's giant sequoia, planted around 1856 by one account, is counted Pennsylvania's largest. Three Painter-era trees are mapped here.
question_answer: The best-known old tree near Media is the giant sequoia at Tyler Arboretum, counted the largest in Pennsylvania by the arboretum and Wikipedia and the state champion since 1950. The Painter brothers planted it around 1856, by one account, inside a planting window the arboretum gives as the 1840s to the 1860s, so it is roughly 170 years old. In 2006 it measured 29 metres tall and 3.93 metres round.
question_context:
Tyler Arboretum keeps what survives of the trees two brothers, the Painters, planted on this ground in the middle of the nineteenth century. Of what they put in, 21 plants of 19 species survive, and the arboretum keeps them as its legacy collection, fenced to protect the roots and marked with blue tags.

The giant sequoia is the famous one. Its central leader was cut off in 1895, which is why it carries several spires, and it is treated every year against fungal disease and fitted with lightning protection. It grows above Painter Road. The ginkgo, behind Lachford Hall, has no published measurements; in November it turns yellow. The Cedar of Lebanon is listed as Pennsylvania's state champion by the Scott Arboretum and Wikipedia, and the arboretum says it is in decline. Its exact spot is not published, so ask at the entrance.

No planting year is recorded for the ginkgo or the cedar, so their ages come from the Painters' window, about 160 to 185 years. Tyler charges admission. The nearest rail is Media station on the Media/Wawa line, several kilometres off, then a taxi or local bus; allow an hour or more from Center City Philadelphia.

faq.a: Not directly. No SEPTA stop serves the gate. Take the Media/Wawa line to Media station, several kilometres away, then a taxi or local bus. From Center City Philadelphia that is well over half an hour, nearer an hour or more door to door.

No. Adults pay $18, seniors $15 and ages 3 to 17 $10; under 3 is free. It is open daily, 9 am to 6 pm from April to October and 9 am to 4 pm from November to March, and closed on Thanksgiving and 24 and 25 December.

faq.q: Where is the giant sequoia at Tyler Arboretum?
faq.a: Above Painter Road. Look for several spires instead of one point, the result of its top being cut off in 1895, and for the fence, blue Painter legacy tag and lightning rod.

trees.name: Tyler Arboretum Giant Sequoia

location.address: Tyler Arboretum, 515 Painter Road, Media, PA 19063

trees.story:
Somebody cut the top off this giant sequoia in 1895, and it answered by growing several new ones. The lost central leader is why it has a cluster of spires instead of the single point its species is known for.

The Painter brothers planted it on the ground that is now Tyler Arboretum, as part of a collection they built between the 1840s and the 1860s. A description of the tree on Wikimedia Commons gives the year as 1856; the arboretum itself only gives the Painters' planting window and says the sequoia may have come from Hoopes Nursery stock. So call it roughly 170 years old, give or take a decade or so.

It is counted the largest giant sequoia in Pennsylvania, and possibly in the eastern United States, by the arboretum and Wikipedia, and has held the state champion title since 1950 by the Commons account. Measured in 2006, it stood 29 metres tall and 3.93 metres round, with a crown spread of almost 11 metres. Those figures are twenty years old.

It has also had care that few trees get. The arboretum keeps it fenced to protect the roots, treats it every year against fungal disease and has fitted it with lightning protection.

It grows above Painter Road. Tyler charges admission, and it is well over half an hour from Philadelphia by public transport, so this is a day out rather than a detour.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its several spires, grown after the top was cut in 1895, and by the fence, blue Painter legacy tag and lightning rod. It stands above Painter Road.

trees.name: Tyler Arboretum Painter Ginkgo

location.address: Tyler Arboretum, 515 Painter Road, Media, PA 19063

trees.story:
Of everything the Painter brothers planted here in the middle of the nineteenth century, 21 plants of 19 species are still alive, and this ginkgo is one of them. The arboretum keeps them as its Painter legacy collection.

The brothers planted between the 1840s and the 1860s on the ground that became Tyler Arboretum. No source gives the year this particular tree went in, so its age can only be read from that window, somewhere around 160 to 185 years. That makes it a good half century younger than the ginkgo at Bartram's Garden in Philadelphia, which arrived from London in 1785.

The arboretum has fitted it with lightning protection and, like its other specimen trees, fenced it to protect the roots. No measurements have been published. If you have measured its girth, tell us.

It grows behind Lachford Hall. Ginkgoes turn a clean butter yellow in late autumn and tend to drop their leaves almost all at once, so a visit in November can catch the crown gold or the ground beneath it covered.

Tyler charges admission and lies well over half an hour from Center City by public transport.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the blue Painter legacy tag, the fence round its roots and the lightning protection. It stands behind Lachford Hall.

trees.name: Tyler Arboretum Painter Cedar of Lebanon

location.address: Tyler Arboretum, 515 Painter Road, Media, PA 19063

trees.story:
Pennsylvania's champion Cedar of Lebanon is in decline, and Tyler Arboretum says so plainly. It may not be here many more years, which is the best reason to see it soon.

The Scott Arboretum's register of Pennsylvania champion trees lists a Cedar of Lebanon at Tyler, and Wikipedia agrees. Neither publishes a height or a girth, so the title stands without a number we can show you.

It is one of the Painter plantings. The Painter brothers planted a collection of trees on this ground between the 1840s and the 1860s, and of everything they put in, 21 plants survive. This cedar is one. No source gives its own planting year, so its age is that window, roughly 160 to 185 years, and every one of those years was spent a long way from the mountains of Lebanon and Turkey where its species grows wild.

The arboretum fences its specimen trees to protect the roots, and this one carries the blue tag of the Painter legacy collection. Its exact spot in the grounds is not published and the pin marks the arboretum as a whole, so ask at the entrance before you set off. If you know the spot, or have a photograph, tell us, while there is still a tree to photograph.

Tyler charges admission and is well over half an hour from Center City by public transport.
